name: Complex regional pain syndrome
populations: people after distal radius or other limb fractures
people after limb surgery or immobilisation
people after crush or nerve injury
summary: Disproportionate, spreading limb pain with sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor and motor or trophic signs after injury or surgery. Diagnosed clinically (Budapest criteria); treatment evidence is low certainty.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Many cases resolve within the first year and a smaller subset becomes chronic (BMJ review); no model reliably predicts the course in an individual

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Function-led and graded; no validated criteria. Return as pain, swelling, range, strength and normal use of the limb allow

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Budapest clinical criteria: sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.68 against non-CRPS neuropathic pain in one validation study of 113 CRPS-I and 47 comparison patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: No test confirms CRPS; tests mainly exclude other causes. Three-phase bone scan: sensitivity 40.0% and specificity 76.5% against the Budapest research criteria in one retrospective series

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Highest incidence in females aged 61–70 years in a Dutch primary-care study; females affected 3.4 times as often as males

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 26.2 per 100,000 person-years (Dutch primary-care database); 3.8% within 4 months of a non-surgically managed wrist fracture in one prospective cohort

overview:
Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a chronic pain condition with a typical clinical constellation of pain plus sensory, autonomic, motor or trophic features that can no longer be explained by the initial trauma; the symptoms spread distally and are not limited to the territory of one nerve [r1,r2]. It usually follows a fracture, surgery or other limb injury, and sometimes a minor injury or none [r3,r4]. CRPS type I has no identified nerve lesion, while type II follows an identifiable nerve lesion [r5]. The diagnosis is made on clinical signs and symptoms alone, using the Budapest criteria, after other causes have been excluded [r2,r1,r6].

The physiotherapist's role is early recognition (especially after fracture or surgery, when disproportionate early pain is the warning sign) [r7], prompt referral for medical review, and graded, function-focused rehabilitation within a multidisciplinary team [r2]. Proposed mechanisms include peripheral and central sensitisation, neurogenic and immune-mediated inflammation, autonomic dysregulation and maladaptive brain plasticity, but no single mechanism has been proven [r4,r2]. The treatment evidence is thin: the 2022 guideline authors describe generally low- to medium-quality research with small samples, and the Cochrane review of physiotherapy rated every comparison as low or very low quality [r8,r5]. This page says where each statement comes from and how weak it is.

epidemiology.text: In a Dutch general-practice database study (1996–2005) the estimated incidence of CRPS was 26.2 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 23.0–29.7). Females were affected 3.4 times as often as males, the highest incidence was in females aged 61–70 years, the upper limb was affected more often than the lower limb, and fracture was the commonest precipitating event (44%) [r3]. After wrist fracture, a prospective cohort of 1,549 patients managed without surgery found CRPS in 3.8% (95% CI 2.9–4.8%) within 4 months, about 1 patient in 26 [r7]. A BMJ review states that CRPS occurs acutely in about 7% of patients with limb fractures, limb surgery or other injuries [r2]. Estimates differ because the populations and diagnostic criteria differ: in the vitamin C trials the heterogeneity was explained by the diagnostic criteria used [r9]. In a multicentre sample of 113 CRPS type I patients, fracture was the commonest initiating event (41.6%) and surgery and crush injuries together accounted for a further 32% [r6].

intrinsic: Female sex, with postmenopausal women at the highest risk [r3]
Intense pain in the first week after fracture: a pain score of 5 or more out of 10 should be treated as a red flag for CRPS after wrist fracture [r7]
Psychological factors such as posttraumatic stress or pain-related fear, which may affect the course and treatability of CRPS [r1]
Genetic and psychological factors are proposed contributors; the sources read did not quantify them [r2]
extrinsic: Fracture, the commonest precipitating event (44% of cases in a Dutch primary-care study); distal radius fracture is the best-studied setting [r3,r7]
Limb surgery and other injuries, including crush injuries [r2,r6]
A nerve lesion, which defines CRPS type II [r5]
Prolonged immobilisation and disuse are proposed contributors (clinical reasoning); the sources read did not quantify their effect

mechanism.summary: CRPS has no single mechanical mechanism. The trigger is usually a limb injury or surgery, most often a fracture, and in some people a minor injury or none [r3,r4]. After the trigger, an aberrant host response to tissue injury is proposed: a prolonged inflammatory and immune reaction, sensitisation of peripheral and central pain pathways, autonomic and vasomotor dysregulation and maladaptive brain plasticity [r4,r2,r1]. These mechanisms are proposed, they probably differ between people and over time, and none has been proven to be causal in all patients [r2].
sequence: A limb injury or surgery occurs. Fracture is the commonest trigger, and a minor injury can be enough [r3,r4].
The early post-traumatic inflammatory reaction, with activation of the innate and adaptive immune systems, dominates the initial phase (proposed) [r1].
Peripheral nociceptors become sensitised, and neurogenic inflammation, in which sensory nerves release inflammatory mediators, adds to swelling and heat (proposed) [r10,r2].
Autonomic changes, including sympatho-afferent coupling and vasomotor dysfunction, alter skin temperature, colour, sweating and oedema (proposed) [r2,r4].
Central sensitisation and maladaptive brain plasticity develop, with cortical reorganisation and body perception disturbance (proposed) [r1,r11].
Pain, sensory change and motor and trophic features spread distally and beyond a single nerve territory [r1].
Guarding, disuse and pain-related fear can reduce movement and use of the limb and may maintain the problem (proposed; clinical reasoning) [r1].
Many cases resolve within a year; a smaller subset becomes chronic, often changing from a warm, inflammatory picture to a cold, autonomic one [r2].

variants.name: CRPS type I (no identified nerve lesion)
variants.description: The larger group. A specific nerve lesion has not been identified; the diagnosis rests on the Budapest criteria [r5,r6].

variants.name: CRPS type II (identifiable nerve lesion)
variants.description: Follows an identifiable nerve lesion, but the pain and signs spread beyond the territory of that nerve. No trials in people with type II met the inclusion criteria of the Cochrane physiotherapy review, so treatment is extrapolated from type I [r5,r1].

variants.name: Warm versus cold CRPS
variants.description: Early CRPS is often warm and red, with inflammatory features dominant; chronic CRPS is often cold and pale or blue, with autonomic features dominant. In one sample those with a cold pattern had a longer median duration (20.1 months) than those with a warm pattern (3.9 months) [r2,r6].

variants.name: Post-fracture and post-surgical CRPS
variants.description: The usual presentation in physiotherapy. Pain that is disproportionate in the first week after wrist fracture predicts later CRPS [r7,r3].

variants.name: Chronic CRPS
variants.description: Visible inflammatory signs fade but pain remains; movement disorders, temperature change, sensory loss, hyperalgesia and body perception disturbance dominate [r1].

anatomy.text: CRPS involves a whole limb and the nervous system that serves it rather than one tissue. Nociceptors and small afferent fibres in skin, muscle, joint and bone signal pain and release neuropeptides; sympathetic efferents control skin blood vessels and sweat glands, which is why colour, temperature and sweating change; the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and the somatosensory and motor cortex process and map the limb (standard anatomy). Inflammatory and immune cells in the injured limb interact with these nerves [r4,r1]. Altered cortical representation of the limb has been described in CRPS and underpins treatments aimed at the brain, such as graded motor imagery [r11].

structures.name: Nociceptors and small afferent fibres
structures.role: Signal pain and release neuropeptides that promote neurogenic inflammation; proposed to be sensitised in CRPS [r10,r2]

structures.name: Sympathetic efferents and skin microvasculature
structures.role: Control skin blood flow and sweating; abnormal control is proposed to cause temperature, colour and sweating changes [r4,r2]

structures.name: Immune and inflammatory cells
structures.role: Drive the early post-traumatic inflammatory reaction through the innate and adaptive immune systems (proposed) [r1]

structures.name: Dorsal horn and spinal cord
structures.role: Site of central sensitisation, in which normal inputs are amplified (proposed) [r2,r1]

structures.name: Somatosensory and motor cortex
structures.role: Cortical abnormalities are described in CRPS; treatment aims to activate the cortical networks that serve the limb [r11]

structures.name: Muscle, joint and bone of the limb
structures.role: Show weakness, stiffness and reduced range, and in some patients altered bone perfusion on bone scan [r6,r12]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
CRPS is a multifactorial disorder associated with an aberrant host response to tissue injury. Biological pathways underlying aberrant inflammation, vasomotor dysfunction and maladaptive neuroplasticity are implicated in its clinical features, and differences in susceptibility to disturbance in any of these pathways probably account for the clinical heterogeneity [r4]. In the initial phase the pathophysiology is dominated by a post-traumatic inflammatory reaction involving the innate and adaptive immune systems. Without adequate treatment, central nociceptive sensitisation, cortical reorganisation and implicit learning processes develop while inflammation moderates, and the main features shift towards movement disorders, changing skin temperature, sensory loss, hyperalgesia and body perception disturbance [r1].

All of this is proposed rather than established. The relative contribution of each mechanism differs between individuals and over time [r2], and the 2022 guideline authors point out that several large trials probably failed because the broad Budapest diagnostic criteria group together a multifactorial, multi-mechanism disease [r8]. Treatment directed at one mechanism may therefore help some patients and not others.

structures.name: Skin and microvasculature
structures.effect: Temperature and colour asymmetry, oedema and abnormal sweating. In one sample, patients with temperature asymmetry mostly had a cold pattern, on average more than 0.6 °C colder than the other limb [r6].

structures.name: Peripheral nerve endings
structures.effect: Sensitisation, allodynia and hyperalgesia; neurogenic inflammation is proposed [r10,r2]

structures.name: Joint and soft tissue
structures.effect: Active range of motion was significantly reduced on the affected side in a CRPS sample, for example wrist or ankle flexion and extension [r6]

structures.name: Bone and perfusion
structures.effect: Three-phase bone scan patterns vary; decreased uptake in phases I and II was associated with CRPS in one study, and a positive scan has a low diagnostic value [r12]

muscles.name: Muscles of the affected limb
muscles.effect: Weakness, reduced active range and movement disorders; tremor or dystonia occur in some patients (clinical convention) [r1,r6]

muscles.name: Disuse and guarding
muscles.effect: Fear of pain and reduced use lead to stiffness and atrophy, which feed back into pain and disability (proposed; clinical reasoning) [r1]

muscles.name: Motor control
muscles.effect: Body perception disturbance and altered cortical representation can change movement planning and limb awareness; graded motor imagery targets this [r1,r11]

cellular.description: The post-traumatic inflammatory reaction, with innate and adaptive immune activation, dominates the initial phase [r1]; in CRPS it is proposed to be exaggerated or prolonged [r4].
Nociceptors become sensitised and sensory nerves release inflammatory mediators, adding to heat, swelling and allodynia [r10,r2].
Altered sympathetic control and sympatho-afferent coupling change skin blood flow and sweating [r2,r4].
Central nociceptive sensitisation, reorganisation and implicit learning develop while inflammation moderates [r1].

cellular.timing: Months to years in some patients
cellular.description: Visible inflammatory signs fade, often to a cold pattern, and pain remains [r2,r1].

systems.effect: Peripheral and central sensitisation, maladaptive brain plasticity and body perception disturbance (proposed) [r2,r1].
Vasomotor and sudomotor dysfunction with temperature, colour, oedema and sweating change [r4,r6].
Post-traumatic inflammation with innate and adaptive immune activation in the initial phase [r1].
Stiffness, weakness, reduced range and trophic change in the affected limb [r6].
Posttraumatic stress and pain-related fear may influence the course and treatability; psychosocial comorbidity should be treated [r1].

grading.system: CRPS type and Budapest decision rules (no severity grading)

grades.description: No specific nerve lesion identified; the large majority of patients [r5,r6].
grades.prognosis: Many cases resolve within the first year; a smaller subset becomes chronic [r2]

grades.description: An identifiable nerve lesion is present, with spread beyond that nerve's territory [r5,r1].
grades.prognosis: No trials in type II met the inclusion criteria of the Cochrane physiotherapy review, so prognosis and treatment effects are extrapolated from type I [r5]

grades.description: Continuing pain disproportionate to the inciting event, symptoms in at least 3 of 4 categories (sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema, motor/trophic), signs in at least 2 of 4 categories at examination, and no other diagnosis that better explains them [r6,r1].
grades.prognosis: Sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.68 against non-CRPS neuropathic pain in one validation study [r6]

grades.description: As above but with symptoms in all 4 categories; intended to reduce false positives in research samples [r6].
grades.prognosis: Specificity 0.79 in the same study, with the lowest sensitivity of the three criteria sets; the advantage over the clinical criteria was small [r6]

timeframes.summary: The course is variable. Many cases resolve within the first year and a smaller subset becomes chronic [r2]. In one sample the median duration was 3.9 months for warm CRPS and 20.1 months for cold CRPS, a cross-sectional pattern rather than a timetable [r6]. Phase boundaries below are clinical conventions.

healing.description: Post-traumatic inflammation dominates; median duration 3.9 months in warm CRPS in one sample [r1,r6]
Many cases resolve within the first year [r2]
Central sensitisation and reorganisation develop as inflammation moderates (proposed) [r1]
Pain persists; median duration 20.1 months in cold CRPS in one sample. Duration is a clinical convention and varies widely [r2,r6]

milestones.label: Pain screen after wrist fracture
milestones.note: A pain score of 5 or more out of 10 in the first week is a red flag [r7]

milestones.label: Vitamin C course ends (prevention trials)
milestones.note: 500 mg daily for 50 days after wrist fracture in the trials pooled by one meta-analysis [r13]

milestones.label: Graded motor imagery programme completes
milestones.note: Two weeks each of laterality recognition, imagined movements and mirror therapy in one trial [r11]

milestones.label: CRPS diagnosed after wrist fracture
milestones.note: The cohort assessed CRPS 4 months after fracture [r7]

milestones.label: Long-term follow-up of graded motor imagery
milestones.note: Pain benefit measured at 6 months in very low quality evidence [r5]

milestones.label: One year
milestones.note: Many cases have resolved; a smaller subset is chronic [r2]

timeframes.returnToSport: Function-led and individual, with no time-based rule. Return to work and sport follows recovery of pain tolerance, swelling, range, strength and normal use of the limb, and may take months. Expect setbacks and plan a graded return with the treating team [r2,r1].

symptoms: Continuing pain disproportionate to the inciting injury, often burning or aching, that spreads distally beyond one nerve's territory [r1]
Sensory symptoms: hyperaesthesia or allodynia (pain from light touch, clothing or air movement) and hyperalgesia [r6,r10]
Vasomotor symptoms: the limb feels warmer or colder than the other limb, with colour change [r6]
Sudomotor and oedema symptoms: swelling and altered sweating [r6]
Motor and trophic symptoms: stiffness and reduced range, weakness, and changes in skin, hair or nails; movement disorders in some patients [r1,r6]
Body perception disturbance and pain-related fear, with reduced use of the limb [r1]
signs: Allodynia or hyperalgesia to light touch or pinprick in the affected limb [r6]
Temperature asymmetry: warm early, cold later; in one sample the cold limb was on average more than 0.6 °C colder than the other limb on infrared thermometry [r2,r6]
Skin colour change or asymmetry (red early, pale or blue later) and sweating asymmetry [r6]
Oedema of the hand or foot, with loss of normal skin creases (clinical convention)
Reduced active range of motion, often more than passive; in a CRPS sample wrist and ankle flexion and extension and elbow or knee flexion were significantly reduced on the affected side [r6]
Weakness, tremor or poor motor control, and trophic change in skin, hair or nails (clinical convention) [r1]

subjective: Inciting event and timing: fracture, surgery, sprain or crush, and the time to the first spread of symptoms; ask about immobilisation and whether pain was settling [r7,r3]
Pain: current and average pain over the last 2 days (0–10), character, spread beyond the injury and beyond a nerve territory, and what touch, movement or temperature changes do to it [r7,r1]

Symptoms in each Budapest category: sensory, vasomotor (temperature or colour), sudomotor and oedema (swelling or sweating), and motor and trophic (stiffness, weakness, tremor, hair, nail or skin change) [r6]
Function and limb use: dressing, grip, weight-bearing, gait; whether the limb feels foreign or hard to move (body perception disturbance) [r1]
Psychosocial context: pain-related fear, posttraumatic stress, sleep, mood, work and compensation (clinical convention) [r1]
Red-flag screen: fever, spreading redness, calf pain, tense compartment, new neurological loss, and any medical history that offers another explanation (clinical convention)
observation: Compare both limbs in a warm room: colour (red, pale, blue), swelling, shine or thin skin, sweating, hair and nail growth [r6]
Limb posture and guarding, protective positioning, and whether the limb is spontaneously used during conversation or dressing [r1]
Tremor, dystonic posture or other movement disorder; visible muscle wasting (clinical convention)
palpation: Light touch, brush and pressure compared with the other limb to find allodynia and hyperalgesia; start gently and stay away from forcing a response [r6]
Skin temperature compared side to side, by hand or with an infrared thermometer; repeat over time because a single reading is less reliable [r6]
Oedema (pitting or firm) and tenderness over joints, bone and muscle (clinical convention)
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive range of the joints of the affected limb with goniometry, compared with the other side; record the pain limit and what limits movement [r6]
Fist and finger flexion by fingertip-to-palm distance, and wrist and ankle ranges, which were reduced in CRPS samples [r6]
Treat provoked pain and fear as findings in themselves; do not force range to prove restriction
strength: Grip dynamometry, comparing sides, and manual muscle testing within pain limits; weakness may be limited by pain and guarding (clinical convention) [r6]
Note poor effort versus fear, and whether strength changes with distraction (clinical convention)
neuro: Map sensory change: allodynia, hyperalgesia, hypoaesthesia and spread beyond a nerve or dermatome; compare with the other limb, face and trunk [r6,r1]
Test the nerves and roots to exclude entrapment, a focal nerve injury or radiculopathy, which can mimic or coexist with CRPS (clinical convention)
Reflexes and sensory testing of the uninvolved limbs to exclude a central or bilateral cause (clinical convention)
Body perception: ask about neglect-like feelings, and consider laterality recognition testing as a baseline for graded motor imagery [r1,r11]
functional: Observe real tasks: hand function, carrying, dressing and weight-bearing through the hand or foot, and the pattern of avoidance [r1]
Gait and weight-bearing for lower-limb CRPS, including use of aids and protective postures
Work and leisure tasks that the patient has stopped, to set graded exposure goals [r14]

specialTests.name: Budapest clinical criteria
specialTests.purpose: Make a clinical diagnosis of CRPS and separate it from other neuropathic pain
specialTests.procedure: Record continuing disproportionate pain; ask about symptoms and examine for signs in the four categories (sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema, motor/trophic); decide whether another diagnosis better explains the picture.
specialTests.positive: Symptoms in at least 3 of 4 categories and signs in at least 2 of 4 categories, with no better explanation. A positive result does not exclude CRPS mimics, so rule out other causes first.

specialTests.name: Budapest research criteria
specialTests.purpose: Select a more specific sample for research
specialTests.procedure: As for the clinical criteria, but symptoms must be present in all 4 categories, with signs in at least 2 of 4.
specialTests.positive: Symptoms in all 4 categories and signs in at least 2 of 4. This set had the lowest sensitivity of the three criteria sets compared, and the advantage over the clinical criteria was small; the abstract does not give a sensitivity value.

specialTests.name: Previous IASP criteria (for comparison)
specialTests.purpose: Show why the criteria were revised
specialTests.procedure: Signs or symptoms alone were enough, and oedema plus disproportionate pain could suffice.
specialTests.positive: High sensitivity but poor specificity, with a risk of false positives and overdiagnosis.

specialTests.name: Three-phase bone scintigraphy
specialTests.purpose: Supportive test, not a diagnostic standard
specialTests.procedure: Nuclear medicine study ordered by a doctor; physio interprets the report only in context.
specialTests.positive: Decreased uptake in phases I and II (D-D-D, D-D-S or D-D-I patterns) was associated with CRPS in one retrospective series (116 patients, 69 with CRPS by the Budapest research criteria). Its diagnostic value was low.

specialTests.name: Side-to-side temperature and swelling comparison
specialTests.purpose: Document the vasomotor and oedema signs for the Budapest criteria and track change
specialTests.procedure: After at least 30 minutes in a room-temperature environment, measure palmar or plantar skin temperature with an infrared thermometer and swelling with figure-of-eight or circumferential measures, on both sides.
specialTests.positive: A consistent side-to-side difference; in one sample cold CRPS was on average more than 0.6 °C colder. No accuracy figures were identified for these tools in the sources read.

clinicalRules.name: Early-pain red flag after wrist fracture
clinicalRules.description: In a cohort of 1,549 patients with wrist fracture managed without surgery, assessed within 1 week, a pain score of 5 or more out of 10 on average pain over the last 2 days should be considered a red flag for CRPS. Pain intensity alone discriminated well (c index 0.98), and a four-item model of pain, reaction time, dysynchiria and swelling reached 0.99 [r7]. This is one cohort, and the rule has not been tested in surgically managed fractures or in other injuries.

clinicalRules.name: No sign or test is diagnostic alone
clinicalRules.description: CRPS is a clinical diagnosis. Supplementary tests mainly exclude other diagnoses [r1,r2].

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain intensity (0–10 numerical rating or 100 mm VAS)
outcomeMeasures.use: Track pain; average pain over 2 days was used as the early-pain screen after fracture [r7]

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain Disability Index
outcomeMeasures.use: Disability measure used as a secondary outcome in a pain exposure physical therapy trial [r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Impairment level Sum Score (ISS-RV)
outcomeMeasures.use: Composite of pain VAS, McGill Pain Questionnaire, active range of motion and skin temperature, used as the primary outcome in a CRPS-1 trial [r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Limb-specific function: DASH for the arm, Lower Limb Tasks Questionnaire for the leg
outcomeMeasures.use: Used as secondary outcomes in the same trial [r14]

outcomeMeasures.name: Neuropathic Pain Scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Used as the pain outcome in the graded motor imagery trial [r11]

outcomeMeasures.name: Goniometry, grip dynamometry and swelling
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective impairment measures tracked at each visit (clinical convention)

imaging.indication: Exclude fracture, malunion, loosening of fixation or other bony causes; not diagnostic of CRPS
imaging.findings: Findings consistent with the original injury; no CRPS-specific finding was quantified in the sources read (clinical convention)

imaging.indication: Occasionally in doubtful cases, on specialist request
imaging.findings: Sensitivity 40.0% and specificity 76.5% against the Budapest research criteria in one retrospective series; the diagnostic value of a positive scan is low [r12]

imaging.indication: Exclude other causes such as tendon, ligament or joint pathology, occult fracture or infection
imaging.findings: Used to exclude alternative diagnoses rather than to diagnose CRPS [r1]

imaging.indication: Suspected focal nerve injury, entrapment or radiculopathy, or to separate CRPS type II
imaging.findings: Identify a nerve lesion that may explain or accompany the pain (clinical convention)

differentials.name: Acute compartment syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Pain out of proportion within hours of fracture, a cast or surgery, with a tense compartment, pain on passive stretch and neurovascular change. A surgical emergency, not CRPS (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Peripheral nerve injury or entrapment
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and sensory loss confined to one nerve's territory with matching weakness; in CRPS type II the pain spreads beyond that territory [r1,r5].

differentials.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Median nerve distribution paraesthesia worse at night, thenar weakness and positive provocation tests; can follow distal radius fracture and may coexist with CRPS (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy or thoracic outlet syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Dermatomal or plexus pattern with neck or shoulder symptoms and provocation findings; no vasomotor and sudomotor change (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Frozen shoulder (shoulder-hand picture)
differentials.distinguishing: Painful stiff shoulder with a capsular pattern; hand swelling, allodynia and autonomic signs point towards CRPS (clinical convention).

differentials.name: Infection, deep vein thrombosis or inflammatory arthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Fever, a raised inflammatory response, spreading cellulitis, calf tenderness or joint-specific synovitis; diagnosis of CRPS requires that no other diagnosis better explains the signs [r1,r6].

differentials.name: Disuse stiffness after immobilisation
differentials.distinguishing: Stiffness and weakness proportionate to the injury, with normal skin signs and pain that settles with use; no disproportionate pain, allodynia or autonomic change (clinical convention).

redFlags: Pain out of proportion, a tense swollen limb, pain on passive stretch, paraesthesia or pallor after fracture, a cast or surgery: treat as acute compartment syndrome until excluded and send to emergency the same day (clinical convention).
Hot, red, swollen limb with fever or systemic illness, a wound, or a prosthesis or hardware: suspect infection and arrange urgent medical review (clinical convention).
Calf pain and swelling, breathlessness or chest pain: suspect deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism and arrange emergency assessment (clinical convention).

Pain score of 5 or more out of 10 in the first week after wrist fracture, or allodynia, swelling or temperature change out of proportion to the injury: tell the treating doctor early and begin gentle, function-focused care, because early recognition is the goal [r7].

New neurological deficit, progressive weakness, bilateral or spreading signs, or neck or spinal signs: refer for medical evaluation, because other causes must be excluded for the diagnosis to hold [r1].

Severe distress, hopelessness, sleep loss or thoughts of self-harm: arrange same-day psychological or medical support, because chronic CRPS is associated with major psychosocial burden (clinical convention) [r1].

management.principles: Management is multidisciplinary and centred on functionally focused therapies, with other interventions used to enable engagement in rehabilitation and to improve quality of life [r2]. Treatment should ideally be matched to the pathophysiology, with pharmacological treatment possibly most effective in the acute stages and invasive methods reserved for specialised centres and carefully evaluated cases [r1]. The evidence is weak: the 2022 guideline authors describe generally low- to medium-quality research in a rare, multi-mechanism disease, and the Cochrane review of physiotherapy found that all comparisons were low or very low quality, with most trials at high risk of bias [r8,r5]. Because the best treatment for an individual is not known, shared decision-making, clear measurement of what works for this person and honest expectations matter more than any one technique.

medical.name: Early recognition and specialist referral
medical.description: Refer early to a pain or rehabilitation physician. Multidisciplinary care centred on functionally focused therapies is recommended, with medical, psychological and physical treatment coordinated [r2,r8].

medical.name: Bisphosphonates
medical.description: In a systematic review of randomised trials, only bisphosphonates gave uniformly positive effects that were significantly better than placebo; reviews also name them as possibly effective in the acute stage. Prescribed and monitored by a doctor [r15,r2,r1].

medical.name: Oral corticosteroids (short course, early)
medical.description: Improvement has been reported with systemic steroids, and they are discussed for the acute stage. Evidence comes from small trials [r15,r1].

medical.name: Topical dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) cream
medical.description: Improvement has been reported with topical DMSO, and the cream is named as a treatment in the acute stage [r15,r1].

medical.name: Neuropathic pain medication
medical.description: Common anti-neuropathic pain drugs can be recommended empirically; no CRPS-specific trial result was found in the sources read [r1].

medical.name: Intravenous ketamine
medical.description: Intravenous long-term ketamine has shown efficacy in randomised trials, but repeated application is demanding and has side effects; specialist use only [r1,r2].

medical.name: Vitamin C after wrist fracture (prevention)
medical.description: Two meta-analyses of the same three randomised trials disagree. One found that 500 mg daily for 50 days, started on the day of injury, lowered the risk of CRPS-I (risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.91; 3 trials, 875 patients; heterogeneity 65%) [r13]. The other found no significant reduction (risk ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.18–1.13; 3 trials, 890 patients; I² 70%), rated the evidence as low quality and explained the heterogeneity by the diagnostic criteria used [r9]. A doctor decides whether to use it.

medical.name: Spinal cord or dorsal root ganglion stimulation
medical.description: Improvement has been reported with spinal cord stimulation, and invasive methods should be used only in specialised centres and in carefully evaluated cases. Dorsal root ganglion stimulation is named as a recent advance [r15,r1,r8].

medical.name: Stellate ganglion (sympathetic) block
medical.description: In the Cochrane review a trial of ultrasound-guided stellate ganglion block versus placebo found no short-term pain benefit in CRPS I (low to very low quality evidence), so it is not supported as a routine treatment [r5].

physio.name: Education and reassurance
physio.description: Explain that CRPS is a recognised condition with a variable course in which many cases resolve within a year; that pain does not mean harm when the limb is moved within tolerable limits; and that the plan is graded return of normal use. Treat psychosocial barriers such as pain-related fear and posttraumatic stress [r2,r1].

physio.name: Graded motor imagery (laterality recognition, imagined movements, mirror therapy)
physio.description: In a trial of 13 people with chronic CRPS1, a programme of two weeks each of hand laterality recognition, imagined hand movements and mirror therapy produced an effect size of about 25 points on the Neuropathic Pain Scale and a number needed to treat of about 2 for a 50% reduction [r11]. The Cochrane review found very low quality evidence from two trials (49 participants) that graded motor imagery may improve pain at 6 months (mean difference −21.00 on a 0–100 VAS, 95% CI −31.17 to −10.83) compared with usual care plus physiotherapy [r5]. A separate review of six trials (171 participants with CRPS type I) concluded that evidence was not sufficient to recommend these therapies over other treatments [r16].

physio.name: Mirror therapy
physio.description: The Cochrane review found very low quality evidence from two trials (72 participants with CRPS I after stroke) of clinically meaningful pain and function improvement at 6 months compared with a covered mirror [r5]. Evidence in post-fracture CRPS is not established, and the review found no trials in CRPS II [r5,r16].

physio.name: Graded exposure and pain exposure physical therapy (PEPT)
physio.description: In a randomised trial of 56 adults with CRPS-1, PEPT (up to five sessions) was compared with conventional treatment. On intention to treat the improvement in the primary outcome was similar (6.7 versus 6.2 points; between-group difference 0.96, 95% CI −1.56 to 3.48), although active range of motion improved more with PEPT. The authors could not conclude that PEPT was superior [r14]. Graded exposure to feared activities is described as part of behavioural therapy [r1].

physio.name: Graded, function-focused physical and occupational therapy
physio.description: Reviews of randomised trials suggest that physical and occupational therapy may help, and multidisciplinary care centred on functionally focused therapy is recommended [r2]. In the Cochrane review, one trial of 135 participants gave very low quality evidence that multimodal physiotherapy improved impairment at 12 months compared with a minimal social work intervention [r5].

physio.name: Desensitisation and sensory re-education
physio.description: Graded exposure to different textures and temperatures to reduce allodynia, usually combined with the rest of the programme. No trial of desensitisation alone was identified in the sources read, and tactile discrimination training was not effective for short-term pain in low to very low quality evidence [r5].

physio.name: Psychological support and sleep, mood and fear management
physio.description: Posttraumatic stress and pain-related fear may influence the course and treatability, and psychosocial comorbidity should be treated and supported [r1].

physio.name: Manual lymphatic drainage, pulsed electromagnetic field and laser
physio.description: In the Cochrane review, manual lymphatic drainage and pulsed electromagnetic field therapy compared with comparators were not effective for short-term pain, and laser gave small, clinically insignificant improvements, all in low to very low quality evidence [r5].

physio.name: Prolonged immobilisation or avoidance of the limb
physio.description: Disuse feeds stiffness, weakness and fear (proposed) [r1]; avoid long periods of rest, splinting or sling use beyond what the original injury needs, and keep the limb in gentle use (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Forced passive stretching or manipulation into provoked pain
physio.description: Forcing range against severe pain can increase pain, fear and guarding; use graded, patient-led movement instead (clinical reasoning).

education: CRPS is real and recognised. It is not imagined and not caused by weakness, and the signs you can see and feel are measurable.
Many people improve within the first year, but the course varies, so we measure progress together and adjust.
Gentle, regular, graded use of the limb is the core of treatment. Pain during graded activity is expected and does not by itself mean damage.
Do not keep the limb still for long periods; keep the joints and fingers moving within comfortable limits and use the hand for light everyday tasks.
Tell your doctor or physio early about burning pain, colour or temperature change, swelling or touch that hurts, especially in the first weeks after a fracture or operation.
Sleep, stress and fear of pain all affect symptoms, and treating them is part of treating CRPS.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation is graded, individual and function-focused, and is coordinated with medical and psychological care. There is no validated staged protocol, so the stages below are a pragmatic framework built from graded motor imagery, graded exposure and functional rehabilitation, with low-certainty evidence behind each part [r5,r2]. Progression depends on how the limb responds (pain behaviour, swelling, allodynia, range and use), not on dates. Doses are common clinical conventions, not trial prescriptions, except where a source is named. Most examples describe an upper-limb presentation after wrist fracture; adapt the same stages to the leg.

stages.name: Settle, educate and keep moving
stages.timeframe: From first suspicion; typically the first 1–3 weeks
goals: Confirm the picture and refer for medical review
Explain CRPS and set a graded plan
Keep the uninvolved joints and the limb moving gently
precautions: Exclude compartment syndrome, infection and deep vein thrombosis first [r1]
Do not force range into severe pain
Follow the fracture or surgical restrictions of the treating surgeon

exercises.name: Education and goal setting session
exercises.cues: Agree two or three functional goals, for example holding a cup or washing the face

exercises.name: Gentle active finger and wrist movement within comfort
exercises.dosage: 5 min every waking hour, 10 slow repetitions each movement
exercises.cues: Smooth, relaxed and below a flare in pain

exercises.name: Shoulder pendulum for stiffness prevention (upper limb)
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang and swing from the trunk; relax the hand

exercises.name: Elevation, relaxed breathing and use of the hand for light tasks
exercises.cues: Use the limb for light tasks rather than keeping it guarded

progressionCriteria: Medical review completed and other diagnoses excluded
Patient can describe the plan and the meaning of pain during graded activity
Daily movement completed without a prolonged flare (settles within about 1–2 hours; clinical convention)

stages.name: Graded motor imagery and desensitisation
stages.timeframe: About 6 weeks; adjust to how the limb responds
goals: Activate the cortical networks that serve the limb without provoking pain
Reduce allodynia and improve limb awareness
precautions: Stop or step back if a task causes a long flare; repeat the previous level
Use a mirror only with the unaffected limb moving; do not force the affected limb [r11]

exercises.name: Hand laterality recognition (left or right hand pictures)
exercises.dosage: Several short sessions daily for about 2 weeks; 10 min each (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Judge as fast and accurately as possible without moving the hand; the order in the trial was laterality, then imagery, then mirror [r11]

exercises.name: Imagined hand movements
exercises.dosage: Several short sessions daily for about 2 weeks; 10 min each (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Imagine the movement, without moving; stay below any pain or swelling reaction [r11]

exercises.name: Mirror therapy
exercises.dosage: Several short sessions daily for about 2 weeks; 10 min each (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Watch the reflection of the unaffected hand; start with the affected hand resting behind the mirror [r11]

exercises.name: Desensitisation with graded textures
exercises.cues: Soft cloth to rougher materials, warm to cool; stay in the tolerable range

exercises.name: Gentle active-assisted wrist flexion
exercises.cues: Support the forearm; slow and smooth

progressionCriteria: Laterality recognition accurate and quick, and imagery tolerated without a flare
Allodynia reduced to a tolerable level and skin handling tolerated
Mirror movement possible without pain increase beyond baseline

stages.name: Graded use and exposure
goals: Return to normal everyday use of the limb
Reduce fear and avoidance through graded exposure
precautions: Increase one variable at a time (load, repetitions or duration); allow 24 hours to judge the response
Use a time-contingent plan with a baseline, not a pain-contingent plan
Do not use loading that provokes a flare lasting beyond the next day

exercises.name: Active wrist extension with light load
exercises.cues: Forearm supported on a table; 0.5 kg or less

exercises.name: Grip squeeze
exercises.cues: Soft ball or putty; smooth squeeze and release

exercises.name: Shoulder flexion raise
exercises.cues: Raise within comfort; keep the hand relaxed

exercises.name: Weight-bearing through the hand: wall lean, then table lean
exercises.dosage: 30–60 s, building to 2–3 min, twice a day
exercises.cues: Share the load between both hands

exercises.name: Graded exposure to avoided tasks (opening a jar, carrying shopping)
exercises.dosage: 10–15 min, once a day, steadily increasing
exercises.cues: Choose the task from the patient's goals; plan the level, not by pain

exercises.name: Lower limb: calf raise and bodyweight squat with full weight-bearing (leg CRPS)
exercises.cues: Even weight through both feet; stay within tolerance

progressionCriteria: Active range within about 20% of the other side (clinical convention)
Limb used spontaneously in daily tasks and weight-bearing tolerated
Budapest signs (temperature, colour, swelling, allodynia) reducing on repeat examination

stages.name: Strength, endurance and return to function
goals: Return to work, hobbies and sport
precautions: Progress load gradually and keep a flare-up plan
Re-refer if signs spread, worsen or fail to improve
Respect the healing status of the original fracture or surgery

exercises.name: Band or dumbbell row
exercises.cues: Smooth tempo; grip without clenching

exercises.name: Incline then floor press-up
exercises.cues: Wrist neutral and loaded comfortably

exercises.name: Overhead press with light dumbbell
exercises.cues: Keep the trunk steady and breathe

exercises.name: Farmer carry
exercises.cues: Equal grip and posture

exercises.name: Work and sport task simulation
exercises.cues: Start with short bouts and build duration

progressionCriteria: Strength within about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Work and leisure tasks completed without a lasting flare
Patient can manage a flare with an agreed plan

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria exist for CRPS; the criteria below are clinical conventions to be agreed with the treating team
Pain, swelling and allodynia at a level that does not limit normal use, with Budapest signs resolved or stable
Active range of motion near that of the other side and normal movement quality without guarding
Strength near the other side (about 90%) on dynamometry, and normal endurance for the task
Completion of graded sport- or work-specific loading with no lasting flare and a flare plan in place
Medical clearance, and psychological readiness, including low pain-related fear [r1]
tests: Grip and limb strength compared with the other side
Pain, swelling and temperature comparison after loading
Sport- or work-specific tasks and endurance

prognosis: Many cases resolve within the first year, with a smaller subset progressing to the chronic form, and that change is often paralleled by a shift from a warm, inflammatory picture to a cold, autonomic one [r2]. CRPS often remains a chronic pain disorder, although the most devastating cases should become rarer with earlier recognition and care [r1]. The sources read did not give a reliable outcome rate for treated or untreated patients. The only validated early signal is intense pain in the first week after wrist fracture, which strongly predicts later CRPS in nonsurgically managed fractures [r7]. Treatment trials are small and often of low quality, so outcomes cannot be promised from any intervention [r8,r5].
prevention: Screen for early disproportionate pain after fracture and surgery, using average pain over 2 days with a score of 5 or more out of 10 as a red flag in the first week after wrist fracture [r7].
Tell the treating doctor early, so analgesia, immobilisation and rehabilitation can be reviewed [r7].

Vitamin C for 50 days after wrist fracture: evidence is conflicting, with one meta-analysis showing a lower risk and another showing no significant difference, so this is a decision for the doctor [r13,r9].
Avoid unnecessary prolonged immobilisation and encourage early graded use of the limb as the fracture or surgery allows (clinical reasoning; not tested for CRPS prevention in the sources read).
Recognise and address pain-related fear and posttraumatic stress early [r1].
clinicalPearls: CRPS is a clinical diagnosis. Count the Budapest categories at the same visit: symptoms in 3 of 4 and signs in 2 of 4, then ask whether anything else explains the picture [r6].
Pain of 5 or more out of 10 in the first week after wrist fracture is a red flag: ask the question, and escalate early [r7].
A bone scan will not settle the diagnosis. Sensitivity was 40.0% and specificity 76.5% in one series, so a normal scan does not exclude CRPS [r12].

The evidence for graded motor imagery and mirror therapy is very low quality but plausible, and the programme is low-risk and cheap. Present it as a trial of treatment and measure the response [r5,r11].
Two meta-analyses of the same three trials disagree on vitamin C. Quote the range (risk ratio 0.45 to 0.54) and leave the decision to the doctor [r13,r9].
Warm and cold CRPS look different and need different explanations. Do not rule out CRPS in a cold, pale, stiff limb [r2,r6].

animation.title: How CRPS can develop after a wrist fracture

captions.text: CRPS usually starts after an injury or an operation. A fall onto the hand is a common start.
She trips and reaches out to protect herself.
The wrist breaks. Fracture is the commonest trigger of CRPS.
Most people recover from a fracture without CRPS. A few do not.
Intense pain in the first week is the early warning sign.
Zooming into the wrist and hand. The drawing is schematic: it shows the proposed process.

actions.text: Abnormal vessel control: colour and temperature change (schematic)

captions.text: A distal radius fracture is the commonest trigger. CRPS can also follow surgery or minor injury.
The bone heals in the usual way. CRPS is a problem of the response to injury, not of the bone.
Inflammation is proposed to be exaggerated and prolonged, with swelling, heat and redness.
Pain nerves become sensitised and sensory nerves add to inflammation (proposed).
Pain is out of proportion and spreads beyond the injury and beyond one nerve territory.
Blood vessel and sweat control are disturbed, so the limb changes temperature, colour and swelling.
Guarding and disuse add stiffness and weakness. Early recognition and graded use help.
Healthy bone. The drawing shows normal fracture healing, not the CRPS process itself.
A haematoma forms and starts the repair.
Inflammation clears debris and normally settles. In CRPS it is proposed to persist, with sensitised nerves (schematic).
A soft callus bridges the gap. The bone usually heals normally in CRPS.
Remodelling follows. The pain, vessel and brain changes can continue after the bone has healed.
